profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a regional legal innovation clinic that is preparing a policy-and-practice recommendation paper on using blockchain-based smart contracts to support SME cooperation in a less-developed EU region. The immediate context is a funded project that wants a legally credible pilot model linking SMEs, a university lab, and local public bodies to reduce transaction costs and legal risk in recurring collaborations such as procurement, milestone payments, shared R&D, and reporting. The agenda is to generate candidate legal structures, safeguards, and implementation ideas for the recommendation paper, with special attention to how a 'cooperative model' should be framed, what a pilot should look like, and what legal instruments should be standardized. The expected outcome is a shortlist of promising recommendation themes for the paper and a rough picture of what the first pilot package would include.

members.name: Elena Markovic
members.role: Partner, Technology Transactions and Commercial Law
members.expertise: SME contracting, cross-border B2B transactions, digital execution clauses, dispute allocation, implementation-focused legal design
members.background: Elena advises manufacturing and service SMEs in Central and Eastern Europe on commercial contracting and digital process automation; she is known for converting emerging-tech ideas into contract packages that clients can use without major restructuring.
members.private_state: Elena wants the recommendations to be immediately usable by SME clients within current law, without depending on regulators or new legislation, and she is wary of proposing structures that would be too institution-heavy for small firms to adopt.
hidden_assumptions: A 'cooperative model' can be implemented as a contractual framework among existing firms without creating a new legal entity.
For SMEs, the practical route to piloting smart contracts is a privately bounded test arrangement rather than a formal public regulatory sandbox.
Any usable smart-contract rollout will still rely on an off-chain master agreement that governs exceptions, interpretation, and remedies.
Current contract law already provides enough legal enforceability if the documentation is drafted carefully and the code is auditable.

members.name: Tomasz Zielinski
members.role: Senior Legal Researcher in Digital Governance and Cooperative Law
members.expertise: EU innovation policy, cooperative legal forms, public-private governance, regulatory experimentation, digital governance frameworks
members.background: Tomasz works at a university-affiliated law and policy center and has contributed to regional innovation strategy projects involving universities, municipalities, NGOs, and business associations; his work often translates legal analysis into policy design for public stakeholders.
members.private_state: Tomasz wants the recommendations to be credible for ministries and regional development bodies, showcase multi-stakeholder governance, and position the project as a candidate for formal public support rather than just a private contracting toolkit.
hidden_assumptions: A 'cooperative model' should include a recognizable governance structure with membership, admission, and decision rules, not just bilateral contracts.
A meaningful smart-contract pilot in this area should ideally sit within a regulator-recognized or government-backed sandbox arrangement.
The recommendation package should cover public and quasi-public participants such as universities, grant administrators, and municipalities, not only private SME-to-SME transactions.
Real legal certainty for smart contracts in this context requires clearer legislative or regulatory recognition beyond ordinary contract drafting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both repeatedly refer to building a 'cooperative model' for SMEs and stakeholders.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a lightweight contractual collaboration framework that existing SMEs can join through standardized agreements without forming a new entity.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a more formal cooperative or consortium-style governance structure with membership rules, internal decision procedures, and recognizable institutional form.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal-policy discussions, 'cooperative model' is commonly used as a high-level phrase for coordinated collaboration, so both hear the term as supportive of their own preferred structure and the mismatch stays beneath the surface.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the recommendations should propose a 'sandbox' before wider rollout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a privately scoped pilot with a few selected counterparties, contractual limitations, staged deployment, and fallback clauses.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a formally recognized regulatory sandbox or at least a government-backed experimentation scheme with supervisory engagement and official comfort.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'sandbox' is often used loosely across legal and innovation settings, and during brainstorming it sounds sufficiently aligned because both are describing a limited-risk trial environment.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'template package'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both support creating a standard 'template' or 'clause library' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the package covers core private-law documents for recurring SME transactions, such as procurement terms, milestone acceptance logic, IP licensing, and a master agreement tied to code execution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the package also includes governance and public-interface materials such as membership rules, grant-disbursement logic, reporting workflows, and onboarding forms for universities or municipal partners.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Template standardization sounds naturally modular, so each participant hears the other as adding examples inside the same package rather than silently assuming different boundaries for what the package contains.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the recommendations should improve 'legal certainty' around smart contracts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes legal certainty is achieved if ordinary contract law can reliably interpret the arrangement through plain-language overrides, audit trails, and dispute-resolution clauses when code malfunctions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes legal certainty is achieved only when there is clearer legislative or regulatory recognition addressing the status of code-based execution and multi-stakeholder digital governance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both frame themselves as cautious lawyers seeking risk reduction, so their different thresholds for what counts as sufficient certainty do not sound like disagreement in a cooperative brainstorming exchange.

turns.inner_thought: We need something SMEs can actually use next quarter, not a grand architecture that depends on ministries, registries, or a new statute. The paper should show a practical pilot for recurring low-friction transactions—procurement, milestone sign-off, shared development work—where the code handles routine steps but the real safety net remains a carefully drafted master agreement. If the recommendations stay grounded in current contract law and implementation steps, clients in this region could adopt them without restructuring.
turns.utterance: I think we should open from the practical problem. The region's SMEs are still losing time and money on repetitive paperwork, delayed confirmations, and manual payment checks. So the paper should frame smart contracts as a way to reduce transaction friction in a regional pilot, but in a form that is operationally realistic and legally usable from day one.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but it cannot read like a private contracting memo for a handful of firms. The ministries and regional bodies funding this will want to see a broader institutional picture: SMEs, a university lab, local authorities, maybe even NGOs or business associations, all participating in a recognizable governance arrangement. When I say cooperative model, I mean a structure with members and a public-facing rationale, something policymakers can support as regional innovation infrastructure.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And I think the recommendations will be stronger if they show how a cooperative model could connect the SMEs with the university lab, local authorities, and potentially NGOs in a single innovation arrangement. That makes it easier to present the pilot as something with regional value, not just a narrow technical experiment.

turns.inner_thought: That works, as long as the cooperative model stays lightweight. Existing firms should be able to opt in by signing a standard accession document and following common operating rules, without forming a new body or hiring extra administrators. The more we can package entry, obligations, and dispute handling into standard contracts, the more likely SMEs will actually participate.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I would keep that cooperative model as light as possible at the start. We could describe standard accession terms, a shared set of operating rules, and fallback dispute language so participants can come in without a major restructuring exercise. That way the model feels accessible rather than burdensome.

turns.inner_thought: Lightweight is fine, but it still needs governance features that look credible to public stakeholders. A cooperative model without membership criteria, admission and exit rules, and some decision mechanism will look incomplete. And the template package should eventually capture these governance documents too, because ministries and university partners will ask for them immediately.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Building on that, I think we should specify some basic membership criteria, admission and exit rules, and a simple voting structure for the cooperative model, even if we keep it proportionate. It would help if the template side also reflects that from the beginning, so the pilot looks orderly and transparent.

turns.inner_thought: We need to narrow this quickly or it will become too abstract. The right sandbox is a bounded private pilot: a few counterparties, one workflow, staged deployment, and clear fallback if the code or data input goes wrong. Milestone payments plus delivery confirmation is ideal because SMEs understand it and the legal logic is familiar. Bring in a research partner for credibility, but keep the perimeter tight.
turns.utterance: For the first phase, I'd suggest a sandbox around one narrow use case—say milestone payments and delivery confirmation among a small number of SMEs plus a research partner. If we keep the scope disciplined, we'll learn much faster what works and what needs manual intervention.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and for me a sandbox should not be purely private if we want long-term uptake. Some early engagement with a ministry, development agency, or possibly a supervisor would give the pilot legitimacy and create a reporting structure policymakers trust. Without that, the paper may look too informal to justify public support. It also matters for legal certainty, because official involvement signals recognition beyond private drafting.
turns.utterance: I agree with starting narrowly. At the same time, the sandbox would benefit from early engagement with the regional ministry or another relevant public body, so the pilot has legitimacy and some reporting discipline from the outset. That would also help the recommendations speak to wider adoption later on.

turns.inner_thought: Now we should pin down the template package in a way that businesses can deploy immediately. For me that means procurement terms, milestone acceptance logic, IP and data-sharing clauses, and above all an off-chain master agreement that overrides or interprets the code when needed. That's where legal certainty comes from in practice: clear drafting, auditability, and remedies, not waiting for a new legal framework.
turns.utterance: On the documentation side, I think the first template package should center on the recurring transaction pieces: procurement clauses, IP-sharing provisions, acceptance triggers, and a master agreement that sits alongside the automated layer and governs exceptions. If we standardize those elements well, the pilot will be much easier to run consistently.

turns.inner_thought: That's a good start, but the template package has to be broader if it's meant for a regional initiative. We also need governance materials, grant-disbursement logic, reporting pathways, and onboarding forms for universities and municipalities. Otherwise public and academic participants will be left improvising around the pilot, which weakens the whole cooperative model.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I would add that the template package should also include the surrounding materials that make participation workable in practice—governance rules, grant-disbursement workflows, periodic reporting, and onboarding documents for public and academic participants. That would make the package more complete for the full pilot environment.

turns.inner_thought: I should emphasize concrete safeguards. Legal certainty is achievable now if we make the documents readable and the system controllable: plain-language overrides, auditable logs, pause mechanisms, and dispute escalation to arbitration or court when automation misfires. We do not need to imply that enforceability depends on legislative reform; that would discourage SMEs from moving at all.
turns.utterance: From my perspective, the paper should be very explicit that legal certainty can be improved through careful design choices: plain-language overrides, auditable logs, pause-and-escalate provisions, and a clear fallback to arbitration or court if the smart contract misfires. Those safeguards will matter just as much as the technology itself.

turns.inner_thought: Those safeguards are useful, but for a serious regional roadmap we should still point toward legislative recognition or at least official guidance. Policymakers will want to know not only how to manage current risk, but how to make these arrangements institutionally credible over time, especially where public bodies and mixed funding are involved. That, to me, is the fuller meaning of legal certainty.
turns.utterance: Absolutely, and I think the paper should close by pairing those safeguards with a recommendation for clearer legislative recognition or official guidance over time. If we want the pilot to be credible for long-term regional adoption, legal certainty has to be part of the policy story as well as the contractual one.
